flashcards.front: Which shift register type converts serial data to parallel, and which does the reverse?
flashcards.back: SIPO (serial-in parallel-out) converts serial to parallel, as at a receiver; PISO (parallel-in serial-out) converts parallel to serial, as at a transmitter.

flashcards.front: What do the mode inputs S1 S0 of the 74194 universal shift register select?
flashcards.back: 00 hold, 01 shift right, 10 shift left, 11 parallel load.

flashcards.front: How does a Johnson counter differ from a ring counter?
flashcards.back: The ring counter feeds Q of the last stage back to the first D input and has n states; the Johnson counter feeds back Q-bar and has 2n states, each decoded by a 2-input AND gate.

flashcards.front: A 6-stage ring counter has how many states, and how many for a 6-stage Johnson counter?

questions.questionText: At the receiving end of a serial data link, incoming bits must be assembled into a parallel byte. The register type used is:
questions.explanation: A serial-in parallel-out (SIPO) register shifts the bits in one at a time and presents the complete word on its parallel outputs; PISO does the opposite job at the transmitter.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit SISO shift register is clocked at 1 MHz. The time delay it introduces between its serial input and serial output is:
questions.explanation: Each bit needs 8 clock periods to travel through 8 stages; T_clk = 1 microsecond, so the delay is 8 × 1 = 8 microseconds.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit register holds 0011. After two left shifts, with 0 entering at the LSB each time, its contents represent the decimal value:
questions.explanation: 0011 (3) becomes 0110 (6) after one left shift and 1100 (12) after the second; each left shift multiplies by 2, so two shifts give 3 × 4 = 12.

questions.questionText: Which type of register loads all its bits on one clock edge and makes them available at once, doing no serial conversion, and is used as a buffer or storage register?
questions.explanation: A parallel-in parallel-out register loads the whole word on one clock and presents it on its outputs immediately; it is the plain storage (buffer) register.

questions.questionText: In a parallel-in serial-out (PISO) shift register, the SHIFT/LOAD-bar control line is used to:
options: Select the direction of shift between left and right
Clear all the flip-flops to 0 asynchronously
Enable the tri-state parallel outputs of the register
Choose between loading the parallel input word and shifting the stored bits out serially
questions.explanation: With SHIFT/LOAD-bar low the parallel inputs are loaded into the flip-flops; with it high each clock moves the stored bits one place toward the serial output.

questions.questionText: How many clock pulses are needed to enter an 8-bit word into an empty 8-bit SIPO shift register so that the complete word can be read on its parallel outputs?
questions.explanation: One bit enters per clock, so 8 clocks put all 8 bits into the register; the parallel outputs are then read directly with no further clocks.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit word is loaded into an 8-bit PISO register (one clock for the parallel load) and then shifted out. Counting the load clock, how many clock pulses have occurred when the last (eighth) bit first appears at the serial output?
questions.explanation: The load clock places bit 1 at the serial output at once; each of the next 7 shift clocks brings one more bit to the output, so the eighth bit appears after 1 + 7 = 8 clocks.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit SISO register (serial input at Q0, data moving Q0 → Q1 → Q2 → Q3, serial output at Q3) is cleared. A 1 is applied to the serial input for clock 1 and 0s afterwards. On which clock pulse does the 1 first appear at the serial output?
questions.explanation: The 1 enters Q0 on clock 1 and moves one stage per clock, reaching Q1, Q2 and Q3 on clocks 2, 3 and 4.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit word is fed bit by bit into an empty 4-bit SISO register, one bit per clock starting at clock 1, and taken from the serial output of the last stage. After which clock pulse does the fourth (last) bit of the word first appear at the serial output?
questions.explanation: The fourth bit enters the first stage on clock 4 and needs 3 more clocks to reach the fourth stage, so it appears at the output after clock 4 + 3 = 7 (in general 2n - 1).

questions.questionText: A SISO shift register clocked at 800 kHz must delay a serial bit stream by 20 µs. The number of stages required is:
questions.explanation: T_clk = 1 / 800 kHz = 1.25 µs; n = t_delay / T_clk = 20 µs / 1.25 µs = 16 stages.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit shift-right register has outputs Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0; the serial input enters Q3 and on each clock the bits move Q3 → Q2 → Q1 → Q0. It starts at 0000 and the serial bits 1, 1, 0, 1 are applied in that order, one per clock. After the 4 clocks Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
questions.explanation: The first bit applied ends up in Q0 and the last in Q3: 1000, 1100, 0110, 1011.

questions.questionText: The same shift-right register (serial input at Q3, bits moving Q3 → Q2 → Q1 → Q0) holds Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 = 1010. With the serial input held at 1, its contents after two clock pulses are:
questions.explanation: Each clock moves every bit one place toward Q0 and puts a 1 into Q3: 1010 becomes 1101 and then 1110.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit PISO register is loaded with Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 = 1101. It shifts right (Q3 → Q2 → Q1 → Q0) and its serial output is Q0. The bits appear at the serial output in the order:
questions.explanation: Q0 is output first (1), then the bits that were in Q1 (0), Q2 (1) and Q3 (1) move to Q0 in turn, so the LSB leaves first.

questions.questionText: A universal shift register such as the 74194 can perform which set of operations?
options: Hold, shift right, shift left and parallel load
Shift right and parallel load only
Shift left and shift right only
questions.explanation: Its two mode inputs select one of four operations: hold, shift right, shift left or parallel load.

questions.questionText: To load the parallel inputs of a 74194 universal shift register on the next clock edge, the mode inputs S1 S0 must be:
questions.explanation: S1 S0 = 00 hold, 01 shift right, 10 shift left and 11 parallel load.

questions.questionText: A 74194 holds QA QB QC QD = 0110. In shift-right mode (S1 S0 = 01) the serial-right input DSR enters QA and the bits move QA → QB → QC → QD. With DSR = 1, the outputs after one clock are:
questions.explanation: Shift right: QA takes DSR = 1, QB takes the old QA = 0, QC the old QB = 1, QD the old QC = 1, giving 1011.

questions.questionText: A 74194 (outputs QA QB QC QD; shift right moves QA → QD with DSR entering QA, shift left moves QD → QA with DSL entering QD) starts at 0000 and receives four clocks: (1) S1S0 = 11 with parallel inputs ABCD = 1001, (2) S1S0 = 01 with DSR = 0, (3) S1S0 = 10 with DSL = 0, (4) S1S0 = 00. The final QA QB QC QD is:
questions.explanation: Clock 1 loads 1001, clock 2 shifts right to 0100, clock 3 shifts left to 1000 and clock 4 holds, so the result is 1000.

questions.questionText: A bidirectional shift register built from D flip-flops chooses between left and right shifting by means of:
options: A 2-to-1 multiplexer at each D input that selects the output of the stage on the left or on the right
An XOR gate that feeds the complemented last output back to the first stage
Two separate clocks, one used for each direction
A decoder connected to the flip-flop outputs
questions.explanation: A mode line drives a 2-to-1 multiplexer in front of every D input; one setting passes the left neighbour's output (shift right), the other the right neighbour's (shift left).

questions.questionText: How many 4-bit 74194 universal shift register ICs are needed to build a 16-bit universal shift register?
questions.explanation: Each 74194 holds 4 bits, so 16 / 4 = 4 ICs are cascaded with common clock and mode lines.

questions.questionText: Two 74194 ICs (outputs QA to QD, shift right moving QA → QD) are cascaded to form an 8-bit shift-right register. The correct connection between them is:
options: QA of the first IC to the serial-left input (DSL) of the second IC
QD of the first IC to the clock input of the second IC
QD of the first IC to the serial-left input (DSL) of the first IC
QD of the first IC to the serial-right input (DSR) of the second IC
questions.explanation: In shift-right mode the bit leaving QD of the first chip must enter QA of the second chip, which is loaded from its DSR input; both chips share the same clock and mode lines.

questions.questionText: A ring counter built from 5 flip-flops has a modulus of:
questions.explanation: A ring counter circulates a single 1 through its n stages, so it has n = 5 states.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit ring counter Q0 Q1 Q2 Q3 (Q0 → Q1 → Q2 → Q3 and Q3 fed back to Q0) is preset to 1000. After 6 clock pulses its state is:
questions.explanation: The single 1 moves one place per clock and returns to Q0 every 4 clocks; 6 mod 4 = 2, so the 1 is in Q2: 0010.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit ring counter has no preset circuit and powers up in the state 0000. It will:
options: Count 0001, 0010, 0100, 1000 like a normal ring counter
Stay in 0000 on every clock, because there is no 1 to circulate
Fill with 1s and then empty, like a Johnson counter
Move to 1000 on the first clock and then circulate normally
questions.explanation: A ring counter only rotates its contents; with no 1 stored it stays at 0000, which is why it must be preset with a single 1 (it is not self-starting).

questions.questionText: Because of a power-up fault, a 4-bit ring counter (Q3 fed back to Q0) starts in 1010 instead of 1000. How many distinct states does it then cycle through?
questions.explanation: Rotating 1010 gives 0101 and then 1010 again, so it alternates between only 2 states instead of the intended 4 one-hot states.

questions.questionText: A 10-stage ring counter is clocked at 1 MHz. Each flip-flop output is a pulse waveform with a frequency and duty cycle of:
questions.explanation: Each output is high for 1 clock period out of every 10, so f = 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz with a duty cycle of 1/10 = 10%.

questions.questionText: A MOD-12 counter is to be built as a shift-register counter. The number of flip-flops needed as a ring counter and as a Johnson counter respectively is:
questions.explanation: A ring counter has n states, so n = 12; a Johnson counter has 2n states, so n = 12 / 2 = 6.

questions.questionText: A Johnson counter built from 5 flip-flops has a modulus of:
questions.explanation: A Johnson (twisted-ring) counter has 2n states: 2 × 5 = 10.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit Johnson counter Q0 Q1 Q2 Q3 (Q0 → Q1 → Q2 → Q3 and Q3-bar fed back to Q0) starts at 0000. After 6 clock pulses its state is:
questions.explanation: The sequence is 0000, 1000, 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, so after the 6th clock the state is 0011.

questions.questionText: In the 4-bit Johnson counter Q0 Q1 Q2 Q3 with the sequence 0000, 1000, 1100, 1110, 1111, 0111, 0011, 0001, which single 2-input AND gate is high only in the state 1110?
questions.explanation: State 1110 is the only state in which Q2 = 1 and Q3 = 0 (the 1-to-0 boundary), so Q2 · Q3-bar decodes it; the other gates are also high in 1100, 1111 or 1000.

questions.questionText: A 5-stage Johnson counter is clocked at 1 MHz. Each flip-flop output is a waveform of:
questions.explanation: The counter has 2 × 5 = 10 states and each output is high for 5 of them and low for 5, so f = 1 MHz / 10 = 100 kHz with 50% duty.

questions.questionText: How many of the possible flip-flop states are unused (never visited in normal operation) by a 5-bit Johnson counter?
questions.explanation: Five flip-flops have 2^5 = 32 states; the Johnson sequence uses 2 × 5 = 10, leaving 32 - 10 = 22 unused.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit Johnson counter Q0 Q1 Q2 is started from 000. Which of the following states never occurs in its counting sequence?
questions.explanation: The sequence is 000, 100, 110, 111, 011, 001; the patterns 010 and 101 are the unused states.

questions.questionText: A 50 kHz square wave with 50% duty cycle is to be obtained from a 1 MHz clock using a Johnson counter. The number of flip-flops needed is:
questions.explanation: The division ratio is 1 MHz / 50 kHz = 20; a Johnson counter divides by 2n, so n = 20 / 2 = 10.

questions.questionText: In a Johnson (twisted-ring) counter, the D input of the first flip-flop is driven by:
options: The Q output of the last flip-flop
The XOR of the last two outputs
The complement (Q-bar) of the last flip-flop
questions.explanation: Feeding back Q-bar of the last stage instead of Q is the twist that doubles the number of states to 2n.

questions.questionText: Which statement about an n-bit ring counter is NOT correct?
options: It needs a decoder to identify each of its states
It must be preset with a single 1 to work correctly
Exactly one flip-flop output is high in each state
questions.explanation: Because exactly one output is high in each state, every output is already a decoded state signal; no decoder is required.

questions.questionText: Besides the two shift registers that hold the operands and the sum, a serial adder needs:
options: n full adders connected in a ripple chain
One full adder and one D flip-flop to hold the carry
One half adder and no storage
questions.explanation: The bits are added one pair per clock by a single full adder; the carry out is stored in a D flip-flop and fed back as the carry in for the next bit pair.

questions.questionText: A serial adder is clocked at 2 MHz. The time needed to add two 8-bit numbers is:
questions.explanation: One bit pair is added per clock, so 8 clocks are needed: 8 × (1 / 2 MHz) = 8 × 0.5 µs = 4 µs.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit serial adder adds A = 0110₂ and B = 0111₂, LSB first, with the carry flip-flop initially 0. After 4 clocks the sum register and the carry flip-flop hold:
questions.explanation: 6 + 7 = 13 = 1101₂, which fits in 4 bits; bit by bit the carries are 0, 1, 1 and the final carry out of the MSB pair (0 + 0 + 1) is 0.

questions.questionText: Compared with a 16-bit parallel adder, a 16-bit serial adder:
options: Is faster because it has no carry propagation
Needs 16 full adders but no shift registers
Uses much less hardware but takes 16 clock periods to form the sum
Produces all 16 sum bits on one clock edge
questions.explanation: The serial adder reuses one full adder for every bit position, trading speed (one bit per clock) for hardware.

questions.questionText: A maximal-length linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) with 4 flip-flops cycles through how many states?
questions.explanation: A maximal-length LFSR visits every n-bit pattern except all zeros: 2^4 - 1 = 15 states.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit register Q2 Q1 Q0 shifts right (Q2 → Q1 → Q0) and its serial input is Q1 ⊕ Q0, so the new Q2 = Q1 ⊕ Q0. Starting from Q2 Q1 Q0 = 001, the state after 3 clock pulses is:
questions.explanation: Clock 1: new Q2 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1, giving 100; clock 2: new Q2 = 0 ⊕ 0 = 0, giving 010; clock 3: new Q2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1, giving 101.

questions.questionText: The all-zero state is excluded from the sequence of an XOR-feedback (LFSR) sequence generator because:
options: The all-zero state causes the flip-flops to oscillate
The register cannot be cleared to all zeros
XOR gates do not accept two 0 inputs
Once in 000…0 the XOR feedback also gives 0, so the register locks in that state
questions.explanation: With all outputs 0 every XOR of them is 0, so a 0 is shifted in on each clock and the state never changes; the generator must be seeded with a non-zero value.

questions.questionText: A shift-register sequence generator must produce the repeating serial sequence 1, 0, 1, 1, 0 (period 5). The minimum number of flip-flops is:
questions.explanation: 2^3 = 8 ≥ 5 suggests 3, but the 3-bit windows 101, 011, 110, 101, 010 repeat 101, so 3 stages cannot tell two states apart; with 4 bits the windows 1011, 0110, 1101, 1010, 0101 are all different, so 4 are needed.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holding 00010110₂ (22 decimal) is shifted right two places with 0s entering at the MSB. The new contents and value are:
questions.explanation: Each right shift divides by 2 and drops the remainder: 22 → 11 → 5, i.e. floor(22 / 4) = 5 = 00000101₂.

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds the unsigned number 10110100₂ (180). After one logical left shift with 0 entering at the LSB, the register holds:
options: 01101000₂ = 104, because the MSB 1 is shifted out
questions.explanation: The shift gives 1 0110 1000, but only 8 bits are kept, so the result is 01101000₂ = 104; the true product 360 does not fit in 8 bits (overflow).

questions.questionText: An 8-bit register holds the two's-complement number 11101100₂ (-20). After an arithmetic shift right by two places (the sign bit is copied into the MSB each time), the register holds:
questions.explanation: Arithmetic right shift keeps the sign: 11101100 → 11110110 (-10) → 11111011 (-5), i.e. -20 / 4 = -5; a logical shift would wrongly give 00111011₂ = 59.

questions.questionText: Which combination of shifts and one addition multiplies an unsigned number N by 10 (assuming no overflow)?
options: (N shifted left 3 places) + (N shifted left 2 places)
(N shifted left 2 places) + (N shifted left 1 place)
(N shifted left 3 places) + (N shifted left 1 place)
questions.explanation: 10N = 8N + 2N = (N × 2^3) + (N × 2^1); the other combinations give 12N, 6N and 9N.

questions.questionText: The essential difference between a register and a counter is that:
options: A register is built from latches, while a counter can only use JK flip-flops
A register has no clock input, while a counter does
A register can hold only one bit, while a counter holds several
A register stores and transfers data words, while a counter steps through a prescribed sequence of states on successive clocks
questions.explanation: Both are groups of flip-flops, but a register's next state is the data applied to it, whereas a counter's next state is fixed by its own present state.

questions.questionText: When a shift register is built from JK flip-flops, each stage (after the first) is connected so that:
options: J = Q of the previous stage and K = Q-bar of the previous stage
J = Q-bar and K = Q of the previous stage
J = K = Q of the previous stage
questions.explanation: With K = J-bar the JK flip-flop behaves as a D flip-flop, so each stage copies the previous stage's output on the clock edge.

subtopics.title: Asynchronous & Synchronous Counters
subtopics.subtitle: Ripple and synchronous counters, modulus, decade counters, frequency division and design

concepts.text: Counters and Modulus

A counter is a sequential circuit that steps through a fixed sequence of states, one step per clock pulse, and returns to the start. The number of states in the sequence is its modulus (MOD). A binary counter made of n flip-flops counts from 0 to 2^n - 1 and is a MOD-2^n counter: 3 flip-flops give MOD-8, 4 give MOD-16. For a MOD-N counter with N not a power of two the number of flip-flops is the smallest n with 2^n >= N, and the extra states are skipped by reset or preset logic; MOD-10 needs 4, MOD-17 needs 5. Ring and Johnson counters are shift-register counters that give only n and 2n states from n flip-flops, whereas a binary counter gives 2^n.

concepts.plainText: 2^n >= MOD, i.e. n = ceil(log2 MOD) flip-flops

concepts.text: Asynchronous (Ripple) Counters

In an asynchronous counter the flip-flops do not share the clock. Each stage is a toggle flip-flop (JK with J = K = 1, or T with T = 1); the external clock drives only the first stage and the output of each stage clocks the next. Using negative-edge flip-flops with the Q output of stage i clocking stage i + 1 gives an up counter: Q0 toggles on every falling clock edge, Q1 toggles every time Q0 falls (every second pulse), Q2 every fourth pulse, and so on. Because a change must ripple through the chain, the last stage settles only after n propagation delays, and during the ripple the outputs pass through false intermediate states (for example 0111 to 1000 briefly shows 0110, 0100 and 0000), which produce glitches in any decoder connected to the counter. The clock period must exceed n × t_pd plus the decoder delay, so the ripple counter is simple and cheap but slow.
Ripple counter variants and limits:
items: Up counter: negative-edge flip-flops clocked from Q of the previous stage (or positive-edge flip-flops clocked from Q-bar).
Down counter: negative-edge flip-flops clocked from Q-bar of the previous stage (or positive-edge clocked from Q); it counts 111, 110, 101, ... 000.
Up/down counter: a mode line selects Q or Q-bar for each stage through an AND-OR (multiplexer) network.
Maximum clock frequency: f_max = 1 / (n × t_pd + t_decode). For 4 stages with t_pd = 25 ns, f_max is about 10 MHz without decoding.
Each stage divides its input frequency by 2, so stage n outputs f_clk / 2^n.

concepts.text: MOD-N and Decade Counters

A truncated-sequence (MOD-N) ripple counter uses a NAND gate to detect the first unwanted state and drive the active-low CLEAR inputs of all flip-flops. A decade (MOD-10, BCD) counter uses 4 flip-flops and a 2-input NAND gate on Q3 and Q1: when the count reaches 1010 (decimal 10) the NAND output goes low and clears the counter to 0000, so the valid sequence is 0000 to 1001. State 1010 exists for a few nanoseconds and the recycle produces a glitch; a small RC or latch on the reset line makes the clear reliable. The same idea gives MOD-6 (reset at 110), MOD-12 (reset at 1100) and so on; alternatively the counter can be preset to a starting value instead of cleared to 0. The 7490 is a classic decade ripple counter, the 7493 a 4-bit binary one.
Synchronous Counters

In a synchronous counter every flip-flop receives the same clock, so all state changes happen simultaneously and there is no cumulative ripple delay or false intermediate state. Steering logic decides which flip-flops toggle: in a binary up counter a flip-flop toggles only when all lower-order bits are 1, so T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0 Q1, T3 = Q0 Q1 Q2. Parallel-carry (look-ahead) wiring uses one AND gate per stage fed directly from the outputs and gives f_max = 1 / (t_pd + t_AND) regardless of the number of stages; serial-carry wiring chains the AND gates and is slower. Synchronous counters can be decoded without glitches and are the choice for high speed, at the cost of extra gates. The 74163 is a 4-bit synchronous binary counter with synchronous clear and parallel load, and the 74160 the decade version.

concepts.plainText: Synchronous binary up counter: T_i = Q0 · Q1 · ... · Q(i-1), T0 = 1

concepts.text: Design Example: Synchronous MOD-6 Counter with JK Flip-Flops
Required sequence 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, then back to 000 (states 110 and 111 unused).
items: Step 1, number of flip-flops: 2^3 = 8 >= 6, so three JK flip-flops Q2 Q1 Q0 on a common clock.
Step 2, state table: list each present state and its next state (000 to 001, 001 to 010, 010 to 011, 011 to 100, 100 to 101, 101 to 000).

Step 3, excitation table: for each flip-flop write the J and K needed for its transition, using 0 to 0: J = 0, K = X; 0 to 1: J = 1, K = X; 1 to 0: J = X, K = 1; 1 to 1: J = X, K = 0. Treat the unused states 110 and 111 as don't cares.

Step 4, K-maps: Q0 toggles every pulse, so J0 = K0 = 1. Q1 sets from 001 but not from 101, so J1 = Q2-bar Q0, and resets from 011, so K1 = Q0. Q2 sets only from 011, so J2 = Q1 Q0, and resets from 101, so K2 = Q0.

Step 5, check: from 101 the inputs are J0 = K0 = 1 (Q0 to 0), J1 = 0 (Q1 stays 0), K2 = 1 (Q2 to 0), giving 000 as required. Also check that the unused states 110 and 111 lead back into the sequence (110 goes to 111, 111 goes to 000), so the counter is self-correcting.

concepts.plainText: f_out = f_in / MOD; output of stage n (n from 0) = f_clk / 2^(n+1)

rows: Only first stage; each Q clocks the next
Wiring only (plus reset gate for MOD-N)

concepts.text: Going Deeper: Counter Design and Timing

Whether a ripple counter counts up or down depends on which edge triggers each stage and which output feeds the next clock. Stage i+1 must toggle when the lower bits roll over: for up counting that is when Q_i falls from 1 to 0, and for down counting when Q_i rises from 0 to 1. So a negative-edge flip-flop driven from Q, or a positive-edge flip-flop driven from Q-bar, gives an up counter; swapping the output used gives a down counter.

Worked example 1: MOD-6 ripple counter, NAND(Q2, Q1) -> active-low CLEAR
Clock  Q2 Q1 Q0
  0     0  0  0
  1     0  0  1
  2     0  1  0
  3     0  1  1
  4     1  0  0
  5     1  0  1
  6     1  1  0  <- lasts a few ns, NAND goes low
        0  0  0  <- cleared; stable states are 0..5
The detected state is 6 (first unwanted), not 5 (last wanted).

A synchronous counter is designed from its state table. Write the present state and the required next state for every count, pick a flip-flop type, fill in the inputs from its excitation table, then minimise each input with a K-map, using the unused states as don't cares. Finally check where every unused state goes: if any unused state leads only to other unused states, the counter can lock out, and those states must be given explicit next states that lead back into the sequence.

Worked example 2: synchronous MOD-5 counter with D flip-flops
Q2Q1Q0 -> next     D2 D1 D0
 000   -> 001       0  0  1
 001   -> 010       0  1  0
 010   -> 011       0  1  1
 011   -> 100       1  0  0
 100   -> 000       0  0  0
 101, 110, 111: don't care
K-maps: D2 = Q1 Q0,  D1 = Q1 XOR Q0,  D0 = Q2' Q0'
Unused: 101 -> 010, 110 -> 010, 111 -> 100 (all re-enter: self-starting)

concepts.latex: T = Q \oplus Q^{+}, \qquad D = Q^{+}, \qquad T_{i}^{down} = \overline{Q_{0}}\,\overline{Q_{1}} \cdots \overline{Q_{i-1}}
concepts.plainText: T = Q XOR Q+, D = Q+; synchronous down counter: T_i = Q0' · Q1' · ... · Q(i-1)'

concepts.text: Truncating a count with a clear input depends on whether the clear is asynchronous or synchronous. An asynchronous clear (7490, 7493 or discrete flip-flops) acts immediately, so the gate must detect N, the first unwanted state, which appears briefly. A synchronous clear (74163) acts only on the next clock edge, so the gate must detect N - 1, the last wanted state, and no glitch state appears. A presettable counter can instead be loaded with a starting value K at each overflow of a 4-bit counter, giving MOD-(16 - K).

concepts.plainText: Cascaded counters: MOD = N1 × N2; duty cycle of an output = (states in which it is 1) / N

concepts.text: Common mistakes with counters:
items: Detecting N - 1 with an asynchronous clear (gives MOD-(N - 1)) or N with a synchronous clear (gives MOD-(N + 1)).
Assuming the MSB of a MOD-N counter has 50% duty: in a decade counter Q3 is high only for counts 8 and 9, so its duty cycle is 20%.
Adding moduli of cascaded counters instead of multiplying them: MOD-5 followed by MOD-8 is MOD-40, not MOD-13.
Using the ripple formula for a synchronous counter: its f_max does not shrink with more stages.

concepts.text: To find the modulus from a given reset gate, find the first count in which all the gate inputs are 1; with an asynchronous clear that count is the modulus. For a synchronous design given as equations, simulate state by state from 000 and count the states until the sequence repeats.

formulas.plainText: Smallest n with 2^n >= MOD gives the number of flip-flops
f_out = f_in / MOD (the MSB or carry output of a MOD-N counter)
n toggle stages divide the clock frequency by 2^n
Ripple counter: settle time n × t_pd; f_max = 1 / (n·t_pd + t_decode)
Synchronous counter: f_max = 1 / (t_pd + t_AND), independent of n

notes.text: MOD-N flip-flop count: smallest n with 2^n >= N. MOD-10 needs 4, MOD-16 needs 4, MOD-17 needs 5, MOD-100 needs 7. Output frequency of a MOD-N counter is f_in / N; each binary stage halves the frequency.

A decade ripple counter is reset by detecting 1010 (the first unwanted state), not 1001 (the last valid state). The NAND gate needs only Q3 and Q1, because 1010 is the first state in the sequence where both are 1.

Ripple counters are asynchronous because only the first flip-flop sees the clock; their delay grows with the number of stages and they produce decoding glitches. Synchronous counters share the clock, need steering logic, and are designed with excitation tables and K-maps.

flashcards.front: Why is a ripple counter called asynchronous?
flashcards.back: Only the first flip-flop is driven by the clock; each later stage is clocked by the output of the previous one, so the count ripples through with a delay of n × t_pd.

flashcards.front: How is a MOD-10 ripple counter made from a 4-bit binary counter?
flashcards.back: A NAND gate on Q3 and Q1 detects 1010 and drives the active-low CLEAR of all four flip-flops, so the counter recycles from 1001 to 0000.

flashcards.front: In a synchronous binary up counter, when does the third flip-flop (Q2) toggle?
flashcards.back: Only on clock edges where Q0 = Q1 = 1, so its input is T2 = Q0 · Q1.

questions.questionText: The minimum number of flip-flops needed to build a MOD-50 counter is:
questions.explanation: 2^5 = 32 < 50 ≤ 2^6 = 64, so 6 flip-flops are needed and 14 of the 64 states are skipped.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit binary ripple up counter starts at 000. After 11 clock pulses its output Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
questions.explanation: A 3-bit counter is MOD-8, so it shows 11 mod 8 = 3 = 011.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit binary ripple down counter starts at 0000. After 5 clock pulses its output Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
A ripple counter is built from positive-edge-triggered T flip-flops (T = 1), with the clock driving the first stage and the Q output of each stage driving the clock of the next. It counts:
options: Up for the first half cycle and then down
questions.explanation: Stage i+1 toggles on a rising edge of Q_i, i.e. when Q_i goes 0 → 1, which happens when the lower bits roll over from all 0s to all 1s, so the count decreases; positive-edge flip-flops need Q-bar as the clock for an up counter.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit ripple counter uses flip-flops with a propagation delay of 20 ns each, and its outputs feed a decoder with a 10 ns delay. The maximum clock frequency is about:
questions.explanation: The clock period must cover the full ripple plus the decoder: 4 × 20 + 10 = 90 ns, so f_max = 1 / 90 ns ≈ 11.1 MHz.

questions.questionText: A 6-bit counter uses flip-flops with t_pd = 12 ns. Built as a ripple counter (no decoding) and as a synchronous parallel-carry counter with AND gates of 8 ns delay, the maximum clock frequencies are about:
questions.explanation: Ripple: 1 / (6 × 12 ns) = 1 / 72 ns ≈ 13.9 MHz. Synchronous: 1 / (12 + 8) ns = 1 / 20 ns = 50 MHz, independent of the number of stages.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit ripple up counter (negative-edge flip-flops, Q of each stage clocking the next) changes from 011 to 100. The false intermediate states that appear briefly on Q2 Q1 Q0 during the ripple are:
questions.explanation: Q0 falls first (011 → 010), its falling edge toggles Q1 (010 → 000), and that falling edge toggles Q2 (000 → 100).

questions.questionText: A binary ripple counter uses flip-flops with t_pd = 10 ns and is clocked at 20 MHz with no decoding. What is the largest number of stages it can have so that every stage settles within one clock period?
questions.explanation: T_clk = 1 / 20 MHz = 50 ns; the ripple takes n × 10 ns, so n × 10 ≤ 50 gives n ≤ 5.

questions.questionText: A decoder connected to the outputs of a ripple counter produces narrow unwanted spikes (glitches). The cause is:
options: The flip-flops change one after another, so the outputs pass briefly through false intermediate states
The flip-flops are all clocked at the same instant
The decoder gates are too slow to respond
The counter skips states when its clock is too slow
questions.explanation: In a ripple counter each stage changes only after the previous one, so a transition such as 0111 → 1000 briefly shows 0110, 0100 and 0000, which the decoder may detect.

questions.questionText: A 32 kHz clock drives a 4-bit binary counter with outputs Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 (Q0 = LSB). The frequency of the waveform at Q2 is:
questions.explanation: Each stage halves the frequency: Q0 = 16 kHz, Q1 = 8 kHz, Q2 = 4 kHz, i.e. f_clk / 2^3.

questions.questionText: A single binary counter must divide a 1 MHz clock down to about 1 Hz or less at its last stage. The minimum number of flip-flops is:
questions.explanation: A division ratio of at least 1,000,000 is needed; 2^19 = 524,288 is too small and 2^20 = 1,048,576 is enough, so 20 flip-flops.

questions.questionText: A MOD-5 counter is followed by a MOD-8 counter, and the first is clocked at 10 MHz. The overall modulus and the frequency at the final output are:
questions.explanation: Cascaded moduli multiply: 5 × 8 = 40, so f_out = 10 MHz / 40 = 250 kHz.

questions.questionText: A MOD-6 counter counts 000 to 101 and is clocked at 12 kHz. The waveform at its MSB Q2 has a frequency and duty cycle of:
questions.explanation: Q2 goes through one cycle per count cycle, so f = 12 kHz / 6 = 2 kHz; it is high only in 100 and 101, 2 of 6 states, a duty cycle of 33.3%.

questions.questionText: A 60 Hz mains-derived pulse train is to be converted into 1 Hz pulses for a digital clock. The counter modulus and the minimum number of flip-flops are:
questions.explanation: Dividing 60 Hz to 1 Hz needs MOD-60; 2^5 = 32 < 60 ≤ 2^6 = 64, so 6 flip-flops.

questions.questionText: A MOD-12 counter is made from a 4-bit ripple up counter by driving the active-low asynchronous CLEAR of all flip-flops from a 2-input NAND gate. The NAND inputs should be:
questions.explanation: The counter must clear as soon as it reaches 1100 (12); 1100 is the first count in which both Q3 and Q2 are 1, so NAND(Q3, Q2) suffices.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit ripple up counter has a 2-input NAND gate on Q2 and Q0 driving the active-low asynchronous CLEAR of all its flip-flops. Starting from 0000, its modulus is:
questions.explanation: The first count with Q2 = Q0 = 1 is 0101 (5); on reaching it the counter clears at once, so the stable states are 0 to 4, giving MOD-5.

questions.questionText: A MOD-13 counter uses asynchronous clearing when the count reaches 13. The highest count that remains stable on the outputs Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
questions.explanation: A MOD-13 counter's stable states are 0 to 12; state 1101 (13) exists only for a few nanoseconds before the clear acts, so the highest stable count is 12 = 1100.

questions.questionText: A MOD-10 counter is to be made from a 74163, a 4-bit synchronous counter whose CLEAR is synchronous (it acts on the next clock edge). The gate driving CLEAR should detect the count:
questions.explanation: With a synchronous clear the counter resets on the clock edge after the detected state, so detecting 9 (1001) makes the next state 0000; detecting 1010 would give MOD-11.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit synchronous presettable counter counts up; when it reaches 1111, the next clock loads 0110 instead of letting it roll over to 0000. Its modulus is:
questions.explanation: The states are 0110 (6) to 1111 (15), i.e. 15 - 6 + 1 = 10 states.

questions.questionText: A binary counter built from 6 flip-flops can have at most:
questions.explanation: n flip-flops give 2^n = 2^6 = 64 states, numbered 0 to 2^n - 1 = 63.

questions.questionText: A decade (BCD) counter starts at 0000. After 27 clock pulses its output Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
questions.explanation: A decade counter is MOD-10, so it shows 27 mod 10 = 7 = 0111; the tens are carried out to the next decade.

questions.questionText: Two cascaded decade counters (units and tens, BCD outputs) start at 00. After 147 clock pulses the tens and units outputs read:
questions.explanation: Two decades form a MOD-100 counter, so the display is 147 mod 100 = 47, i.e. tens 0100 and units 0111; 1001 0011 is 147 in hexadecimal.

questions.questionText: The 7490 decade ripple counter IC is made internally of:
options: A divide-by-8 section and a divide-by-2 section
A divide-by-2 section and a divide-by-5 section
questions.explanation: The 7490 contains one flip-flop (÷2) and a three-flip-flop ÷5 counter; joining them gives ÷10.

questions.questionText: The MSB output Q3 of a decade (BCD) counter 0000–1001 is fed by a 50 kHz clock. The frequency and duty cycle of Q3 are:
questions.explanation: Q3 completes one cycle per 10 clocks, f = 50 kHz / 10 = 5 kHz; it is 1 only in the counts 8 and 9, 2 of 10 states, so the duty cycle is 20%.

questions.questionText: The main advantage of a synchronous counter over a ripple counter is that:
options: It needs no logic gates besides the flip-flops
It uses fewer flip-flops for the same modulus
All flip-flops change together, so there is no cumulative delay and the counter can run faster
Only the first flip-flop needs a clock connection
questions.explanation: A common clock makes the settling time one flip-flop delay (plus gating) regardless of the number of stages.

questions.questionText: In a 3-bit synchronous binary DOWN counter built from T flip-flops (Q0 = LSB), the T input of the Q2 flip-flop must be:
questions.explanation: When counting down a bit toggles only when all lower bits are 0 (a borrow), for example 100 → 011, so T2 = Q0-bar · Q1-bar; Q0 · Q1 is the up-counter condition.

questions.questionText: For a JK flip-flop that must go from Q = 1 to Q+ = 0 on the next clock, the excitation table requires:
questions.explanation: Either reset (J = 0, K = 1) or toggle (J = 1, K = 1) takes Q from 1 to 0, so J is a don't care and K must be 1.

questions.questionText: In designing a synchronous counter with D flip-flops, the D input needed for each flip-flop is:
options: The complement of the present state Q
1 whenever the flip-flop must change state, otherwise 0
Equal to that flip-flop's desired next state Q+
Always a don't care for unused states only
questions.explanation: A D flip-flop copies D on the clock edge, so its excitation is simply D = Q+; the 'change / no change' rule describes a T flip-flop.

questions.questionText: For a T flip-flop, the T values needed for the transitions 0 → 1 and 1 → 1 are respectively:
questions.explanation: T = 1 makes the flip-flop toggle (0 → 1) and T = 0 holds it (1 → 1); in general T = Q ⊕ Q+.

questions.questionText: A 2-bit synchronous counter with D flip-flops must follow the Gray-code sequence Q1 Q0 = 00 → 01 → 11 → 10 → 00. The required input equations are:
questions.explanation: From the state table, Q1+ is 0, 1, 1, 0 for Q1Q0 = 00, 01, 11, 10, which equals Q0; Q0+ is 1, 1, 0, 0, which equals Q1-bar. D = Q+ for D flip-flops.

questions.questionText: A synchronous counter has JK flip-flops Q2 Q1 Q0 with J0 = Q2-bar, K0 = 1; J1 = K1 = Q0; J2 = Q1 · Q0, K2 = 1. Starting from Q2 Q1 Q0 = 000, its modulus is:
questions.explanation: Applying the JK rules gives 000 → 001 → 010 → 011 → 100 → 000 (from 100, J0 = 0 and J2 = 0, K2 = 1 reset everything), so there are 5 states.

questions.questionText: A counter is said to suffer from lock-out when:
options: It stops counting because the clock frequency is too high
Its reset input is held permanently active
After entering an unused state it keeps cycling among unused states and never returns to the intended sequence
Two flip-flops change state at the same clock edge
questions.explanation: Lock-out is avoided by specifying the next states of the unused states (instead of leaving them all as don't cares) so that each leads back into the main sequence.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit Johnson counter (Q0 ← Q2-bar, Q1 ← Q0, Q2 ← Q1) normally counts Q2 Q1 Q0 = 000, 001, 011, 111, 110, 100. If noise puts it into 010, it will:
options: Alternate between 010 and 101 indefinitely, a lock-out condition
Return to 000 on the next clock
Go to 011 and then continue in the normal sequence
questions.explanation: From 010 the next state is Q2 = Q1 = 1, Q1 = Q0 = 0, Q0 = Q2-bar = 1, i.e. 101, and from 101 it returns to 010, so the counter is locked out of its main sequence.

questions.questionText: A state diagram for a 2-bit synchronous up/down counter with one mode input M is drawn. How many transition arrows does it contain in total?
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 states has one outgoing arrow for M = 0 (down) and one for M = 1 (up), giving 4 × 2 = 8 arrows.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit synchronous up/down counter holds 101. It counts down for 3 clock pulses and then up for 1 clock pulse. Its final state is:
In a 4-bit synchronous binary up counter with parallel carry (T0 = 1, T1 = Q0, T2 = Q0 Q1, T3 = Q0 Q1 Q2), how many AND gates are needed?
questions.explanation: T0 is tied to 1 and T1 is wired straight to Q0; only T2 (a 2-input AND) and T3 (a 3-input AND) need gates.

questions.questionText: Which statement about counters is NOT correct?
options: The maximum clock frequency of a ripple counter does not depend on the number of stages
A synchronous counter applies the clock to all flip-flops at the same time
A ripple counter needs no steering logic between its stages
Designing a synchronous counter uses a state table and flip-flop excitation tables
questions.explanation: A ripple counter's settling time is n × t_pd, so its maximum frequency falls as stages are added; the other statements are correct.

questions.questionText: The modulus of a counter is:
options: The highest count it can display
The number of flip-flops in the counter
The ratio of its maximum clock frequency to its output frequency
The number of distinct states it passes through before the sequence repeats
questions.explanation: A MOD-N counter has N states; its highest count is N - 1, which is a common confusion.

questions.questionText: A ripple counter is classed as asynchronous because:
options: It has no clock input at all
Its flip-flops are not all clocked by the same clock signal
Its flip-flops use asynchronous preset inputs to count
Its output is not related to the clock frequency
questions.explanation: Only the first stage sees the external clock; every other stage is clocked by the output of the stage before it.

questions.questionText: A MOD-6 up counter starts at 000. After 20 clock pulses it reads Q2 Q1 Q0 =
questions.explanation: The counter repeats every 6 pulses, so it reads 20 mod 6 = 2 = 010.

questions.questionText: A decade (MOD-10) down counter starts at 0000 and receives 13 clock pulses. Its output Q3 Q2 Q1 Q0 is:
questions.explanation: Counting down from 0 goes 9, 8, 7, …; after 13 pulses it shows (0 - 13) mod 10 = 7 = 0111.

questions.questionText: A synchronous counter that follows a Gray-code sequence is preferred when its outputs drive a decoder because:
options: It needs fewer flip-flops than a binary counter
Only one flip-flop changes per clock, so no false intermediate codes can reach the decoder
It can run with no clock
It counts twice as fast as a binary counter
questions.explanation: In binary, several bits may change at once and slightly different delays can produce momentary wrong codes; Gray code changes one bit per step.

questions.questionText: A MOD-6 synchronous counter (000 to 101) is clocked at 12 kHz. The frequency of the waveform at its LSB Q0 is:
questions.explanation: Q0 alternates 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1 through the six states and the pattern continues without a break at the recycle, so it toggles every clock: 12 kHz / 2 = 6 kHz.

questions.questionText: A counter must count from 0 to 99. The number of flip-flops needed as a pure binary counter and as two cascaded BCD decade counters is respectively:
questions.explanation: Binary: 100 states need 2^7 = 128 ≥ 100, so 7; BCD: each decade needs 4 flip-flops, so 2 × 4 = 8.

questions.questionText: A 4-bit binary up counter holds 1111 and receives one more clock pulse. Its next state is:
questions.explanation: A 4-bit counter is MOD-16, so 15 + 1 wraps to 0 = 0000 (a carry-out is produced).

questions.questionText: In an asynchronous (ripple) binary counter, the external clock pulses are applied to:
options: Every flip-flop at the same time
The CLEAR inputs of all flip-flops
questions.explanation: The clock drives only the LSB stage; each following stage is clocked by the output of the stage before it.
